analysis.one_liner: Repeals the federal tax credit for donations that fund private school scholarships.
analysis.headline: A Senate bill with 34 cosponsors to repeal the private school scholarship tax credit has sat in the Senate Finance Committee since April 2026 with no hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would delete the new federal income tax credit — created in 2025 — that gives taxpayers a dollar-for-dollar credit, up to $1,700 per year, for donations to scholarship organizations that pay private school tuition. It would also strike the rule that lets families exclude those scholarship amounts from taxable income. Sponsors describe the goal in the bill's title: keep public money in public schools. The bill has never gotten a hearing in the Senate Finance Committee, where it has sat since it was introduced.
analysis.who_benefits: If the bill passed, public school systems would keep an alternative funding channel from opening, and the federal Treasury would not forgo revenue on donations routed to private school tuition. Public education advocates argue the tax credit effectively converts federal revenue into private school subsidies, and that repeal protects resources and accountability for the roughly 90% of students in public schools.

how_it_helps.text: The bill strikes section 25F of the tax code, ending the federal income tax credit for individual contributions to scholarship granting organizations, which reimburse donations of up to $1,700 per year to fund private school scholarships [S2].
It also strikes section 139K, removing the rule that excludes scholarship amounts from SGOs from a family's taxable income [S2].

The repeal takes effect for tax years ending after December 31, 2026 — meaning it would shut down the credit before most donations under the program could generate tax credits, since the credit is scheduled to become usable in 2027 [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Families who would have used SGO scholarships to pay private school tuition would lose that funding stream, and private schools — including religious schools, the main users of such programs — would lose a new federal subsidy pipeline. Donors who give to scholarship organizations would lose the dollar-for-dollar tax credit.

drawbacks.text: Repeal ends a new source of private school scholarships before it starts; scholarship organizations under the 2025 program can prioritize low-income students, and some families would lose an option to leave public schools they are dissatisfied with [S2].

Private schools and school choice advocates argue the credit expands educational options rather than draining existing public funding, since donations are voluntary; the bill eliminates the program entirely rather than reforming it, such as by adding accountability rules [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill protects public school funding and federal revenue, and sponsors frame it as stopping a new subsidy for private education before it scales up. The genuine cost falls on families who would have used the scholarships and on school choice advocates' goal of broader private options. There is no middle path in the bill — it is a full repeal, effective before the credit's first usable year — so families wanting scholarships would get nothing, not a reformed version.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in April 2026 and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it has sat for months without a hearing, a markup, or any vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Mark Kelly introduced the bill on April 15, 2026, with 30 original cosponsors, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance [S2].
The bill has 34 cosponsors: 32 of the 45 Senate Democrats and both independents, including Minority Leader Chuck Schumer [S3].
The full action history shows only two entries: introduction and referral to Finance; no committee action, hearing, floor vote, or House companion has occurred [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill has stalled, the private school sector and school choice advocates keep the 2025 federal tax credit on the books and free to begin operating in 2027. Supporters of public schools get nothing from this Congress so far.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private school and school choice advocates

sides.party_line_note: All 34 cosponsors are Democrats or independents — 32 of 45 Democrats plus both independents — and no Republican has signed on, matching the fact that the 2025 tax credit it would repeal was enacted by Republican majorities.

industries.industry: Private K-12 schools, including religious schools
industries.note: The 2025 tax credit creates a federal subsidy pipeline: donors get their donations reimbursed up to $1,700, and schools receive tuition revenue from the scholarship organizations. Repeal would shut that pipeline before it starts, keeping tuition dollars and most students in the public system.

These nonprofits exist to collect donations and pay private school tuition; the bill deletes both their tax credit and the tax exemption for the scholarships they hand out, eliminating their reason to exist under the federal program [S2].

Anyone giving to a scholarship organization currently would get a dollar-for-dollar federal credit up to $1,700 per year. Repeal means donations to private school scholarships receive no federal reimbursement.
Public schools keep students and the tax revenue that the credit would have directed toward private tuition instead of the Treasury, which is the outcome the bill's title describes.

analysis.trajectory: The Congress runs through January 3, 2027, but a bill with no Republican support, no hearing, and no markup after months in the Senate Finance Committee is very unlikely to advance. The realistic path is that it dies in committee when this Congress ends, unless sponsors attach it to unrelated must-pass tax legislation, which is rare for a repeal opposed by the chamber's majority.
